title: Not Sleeping This Winter
summary: Bruno decides he will not sleep through winter this year, because he wants to see the snow with his own eyes.

scenes.text:
Autumn came to the Tall Pines Forest smelling of wet earth and sweet apples. Down through the air, one after another, came the leaves. They made a soft sound when somebody stepped on them, and they covered the path in yellow and red. Over everything else passed the wind. It moved the branches and pushed fat clouds across the sky, as if it were sweeping summer away to store it in a drawer.

In every cave and burrow there was a rush. The marmots carried seeds. The dormice fluffed up beds of moss. The turtles looked for the softest mud in the stream.

"To sleep, to sleep!" they all sang. "Winter is on its way!"

And in the middle of all that yawning stood Bruno, a brown bear with big paws, round ears, and a belly that sounded like a drum when he scratched it. Bruno had a dry leaf stuck on his nose and a brand-new idea spinning around in his head. An idea he did not yet dare to say out loud.

"I'm not going to hibernate this year," announced Bruno.

His grandmother, Rosalinda the bear, stopped arranging dry leaves and looked at him with very wide eyes.

"You're not going to sleep? But sweetheart, we bears sleep all winter long. It's what we do."

"I want to see winter," said Bruno. "Everybody tells me about it and nobody looks at it. They say the sky turns white and the water turns hard. I want to see it with my own eyes!"

Rosalinda looked at him fondly and out slipped a laugh. It was a warm, round sound, like river water in summer.

"All right," she said. "But eat a lot, a lot, a lot. And in case you change your mind, don't fully close the door."

Bruno ate blueberries until his tongue was painted blue. Then he sat down at the mouth of the cave, crossed his paws, and waited for winter the way you wait for a friend who is coming from far away.

The first days of winter were a party. The forest went so quiet that Bruno could hear his own footsteps: crish, crish, crish over the frost. Every puddle along the path had turned hard as a plate, and when Bruno stepped on it carefully there was a crunch. Crick! That little noise made him laugh and laugh.

"I'm awake and the puddle is asleep!" he giggled to himself.

He discovered things no sleepy bear had ever seen: the white steam that came out of his mouth like smoke from a kettle, the spiderwebs turned into crystal necklaces, the pale, lazy sun peeking late between the pines. He ate the last frozen blackberries, which tasted like forest ice cream.

At night he wrapped himself in his moss blanket at the mouth of the cave and told his grandmother about his day, and she answered with one very long snore from deep inside.

One night Bruno woke up because the silence had changed its sound. He came out of the cave and stood completely still, with his mouth open.

Thousands of white dots were coming down from the sky, spinning slowly, in no hurry at all. They landed on his nose, on his ears, on his shoulders, and they made no noise: only a cold, soft tickle, as if the air were full of feathers.

"And what is this?" he whispered.

"Snow," answered a small voice from a branch.

Bruno didn't look to see who it was. He couldn't stop looking up. Behind the clouds, round and yellow, shone the moon. And between the flakes slipped two or three stars. They all seemed to wink at him.

He sat down on the ground. The snow covered his paws, his belly, the tip of his tail. Bruno laughed so hard that the snow shook off him, and he thought that staying awake had been worth it.

In the morning, the forest lake was not water anymore: it was a mirror. Bruno put one paw on it very, very carefully. Then the other one. Then all four.

And then, whoops! He slipped and landed on his belly with a thud. It sounded like a drum full of snow.

"Again!" he shouted, delighted.

Bruno learned to skate in the funniest way possible: by falling over. He slid backwards, sideways, spinning like a leaf on the water, with all four paws up in the air. From the forest came laughter: a hare, two squirrels, and a whole crowd of birds had come to watch the show of the skating bear.

"Bears don't skate!" said the hare.

"This one does," answered Bruno, and he fell over again, and everyone laughed again, and the ice made a funny noise, tuck, tuck, tuck, as if it were laughing underneath too.

And that is how Bruno made winter friends: the ones who don't hibernate.

He met Frida, the hare with the white fur, who taught him to walk on top of the snow without sinking. He met the three sparrows on the crooked branch, who slept all squished together like a single pom-pom. He met Tomas, the fox with the enormous tail, who showed him where the stream was still singing under the ice.

And right at the top, in the old oak, lived Ulises. He was big, he was serious, and he had eyes as round as two coins: an owl. He said important things in a whisper:

"Hoooo... Bruno... winter is beautiful, and it is also hard. When the forest warns you, listen to it."

"And how does it warn me?" asked Bruno.

"It goes quiet," said Ulises. "Quieter than now."

Bruno didn't understand, but he nodded his head, because it was night and because he was very happy. They all ate pine nuts and told stories until the snow turned blue.

One afternoon the forest went quiet. So quiet that Bruno could hear his own heart. He remembered Ulises and felt a strange tickle in his belly.

Then came the wind. Not the gentle, warm one from before: this one came strong, pushing the snow sideways, erasing the paths, whistling through the pines like an enormous flute. Far away, behind the mountains, a long thunder rolled, as if the sky were stretching.

Bruno walked and walked, but everything looked the same: white, white, white. His paws were stiff with cold. His nose was freezing. And most of all, he had an enormous sleepiness, a sleepiness that weighed on his eyelids like two warm stones.

"I'll just close my eyes for a moment," he said, and he sat down beside a fallen trunk.

And from somewhere in the snow, very close by, somebody called him by his name.

It was Frida and Tomas, with snow up to their ears.

"Up you get, bear!" said the hare. "You can't sleep here."

They pushed him and pulled him and carried him between the two of them all the way to the old oak. Tomas pushed aside some roots and a little moss, and behind them appeared a door. The three of them squeezed into the burrow, which was small, dark, and as warm as a cup of milk.

Inside there were piles of dry grass, stored seeds, and three sparrows asleep in a corner. Ulises was waiting for them with shining eyes.

Lila covered Bruno with her own body and with a big pile of leaves. Tomas laid his enormous tail over Bruno's cold paws. Outside, the wind kept whistling, but inside you could hear something else: the breathing of friends, all close together, all in the same rhythm.

"Thank you," said Bruno, his voice thick with sleep.

"That's what winter friends are for," said Tomas. "For lending you a tail."

When the storm calmed down, the sun peeked out again and the forest was covered in sugar. Bruno came out of the burrow, stretched, and discovered something curious: everything felt heavy. His paws, his head, even his whiskers.

"I think my body is telling me something," he said slowly.

He sat down in the snow and breathed. He did it deeply, once, twice, three times, the way you do before something important. And then he understood: his body was not stubborn or boring. His body was wise. It was asking him to rest because it loved him, just as Frida asked him to eat and Ulises asked him to listen.

"I've seen winter. I saw the snow, I skated, I made friends. Now it's my turn to sleep," he said in a whisper.

Ulises ruffled his feathers, pleased.

"Hoooo... that, Bruno, is called growing up."

Lila gave him a hare hug, which are quick hugs. Tomas gave him a pine nut for the road. Bruno promised to come back in spring.

The walk home was slow and lovely. Bruno left great big round footprints, and inside each one a blue shadow gathered.

Grandmother Rosalinda didn't even move when he came in. Bruno arranged the dry leaves, turned around three times on his bed of moss, the way bears do, and lay down with his belly facing up.

From the mouth of the cave he could see a piece of sky. There it was, white and calm, the moon. The snow was shining as if somebody had saved the whole day on the ground so that it would not be lost.

Bruno closed his eyes. He thought about the ice, about the laughing, about the tail of Tomas. He thought that winter was even more beautiful than everyone had told him.

And then, very slowly and very warmly, out slipped his first snore.

Outside it kept snowing. Inside, a happy bear slept until spring.
